title: Vulnerability giving attackers full control of Macs is under active exploitation
gist: The Netherlands NCSC reports active in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-65400, a macOS screen-sharing state-management flaw patched by Apple last week for Tahoe, Sequoia and Sonoma, in which attackers reaching port 5900 over the Internet gained root and installed Monero miners.

insights.claim: The Netherlands National Cyber Security Centrum has observed active abuse of a macOS vulnerability on multiple systems where port 5900 was reachable from the Internet, with root access obtained and a Monero crypto miner placed in every observed case.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Confirmed in-the-wild root compromise of Macs moves this from theoretical risk to an active incident-response item for any fleet with screen sharing enabled.
insights.quote: In all these cases, root had been accessed on the affected system and a Monero crypto miner had been placed.

insights.claim: Current exploitation is limited to Monero mining payloads that harvest Mac compute for the attacker, with no indications of anything else being installed so far.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Cryptojacking remains the default monetization for opportunistic root access, which keeps Monero's privacy properties structurally tied to commodity malware economics.
insights.locator: Right now, there are no indications exploits are being used

insights.claim: The larger risk is that attackers pivot from mining to installing credential-stealing malware or other more nefarious payloads using the same root access.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The same access path already proven at scale can be resold or repurposed, so today's low-severity payload understates the true exposure.
insights.quote: A bigger risk is that attackers might exploit the vulnerability to install malware that steals credentials or performs other more nefarious activities.
insights.locator: Right now, there are no indications exploits are being used

themes.theme: The flaw and Apple's disclosure posture

insights.claim: CVE-2026-65400 carries a severity rating of 7.1 out of 10 and stems from a state-management bug in the macOS screen sharing feature, which lets a remote party view the screen and control keyboard and mouse.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A mid-range CVSS score is being exploited at root level in the wild, a reminder that severity scores are a poor proxy for real-world exploitation risk.
insights.locator: Do you know if your screen sharing is on?

insights.claim: Apple patched the flaw last week across macOS Tahoe, Sequoia and Sonoma, and details became public at the Black Hat security conference.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Exploitation followed conference disclosure almost immediately — the patch-to-exploit window for publicly demoed bugs is now effectively days.

insights.claim: Apple hedged its disclosure by saying the vulnerability 'may' allow an uncredentialed attacker to gain access, which the author notes is common softening language among tech developers.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Vendor advisory language systematically understates severity, so risk teams should weight independent CERT reporting over vendor phrasing.
insights.quote: It’s unclear why Apple hedged, but softening language is common among most tech developers when disclosing vulnerabilities.
insights.locator: Apple said last week that CVE-2026-65400

themes.theme: Default-open configuration as the root cause

insights.claim: Enabling macOS screen sharing causes the built-in macOS firewall to open port 5900, creating the exposed attack surface automatically without an explicit user decision to expose it.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Insecure-by-default feature design, not user error, is generating the exposed population — a durable pattern in consumer OS security incidents.
insights.quote: When screen sharing is turned on, the macOS firewall opens the port.

insights.claim: The recommended mitigations — connecting over a VPN or SSH tunneling instead of exposing port 5900 — require actions beyond the capabilities of most users, leaving the safest practical advice as toggling screen sharing off between sessions.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The usability gap between expert-grade mitigation and consumer capability is precisely the gap managed security and endpoint vendors monetize.
insights.quote: The alternatives require actions that aren’t within the capabilities of most users.
insights.locator: Security practitioners generally advise Mac users

insights.claim: Routers and dedicated firewalls generally block port 5900 unless configured to override that default, meaning the exploited population is concentrated among machines with deliberately or accidentally opened network paths.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Bounds the blast radius: exposure correlates with misconfigured network edges rather than the whole macOS install base.
insights.locator: Routers and dedicated firewalls generally block the port
